subject: English
topic: Spotting Errors VI — Subject-Verb Agreement, Tense, Modifiers and Idioms (W13 B1)

questions.stem: Each of the students in the classroom (A) / have submitted (B) / their assignment on time (C). / No error (D).
questions.explanation: B is correct. Error in Part B: 'have submitted' should be 'has submitted'. RULE: 'Each of' + plural noun still takes a SINGULAR verb because 'Each' is the head pronoun and it is singular. Compare: 'Each of the boys HAS done his work.' Similarly, 'their' in part C should ideally be 'his/her' (though SSC increasingly accepts 'their' for singular reference). Primary error = B. TRAP: Students see 'students' (plural) immediately before the verb and write 'have'. The trick is to identify the REAL subject = 'Each' (singular).

questions.stem: She has been working (A) / on this project (B) / since three years (C). / No error (D).
questions.explanation: C is correct. Error in Part C: 'since three years' should be 'for three years'. RULE: SINCE = used with a specific POINT in time ('since 2020', 'since Monday', 'since morning'). FOR = used with a PERIOD/DURATION of time ('for three years', 'for two hours', 'for a long time'). 'Three years' is a duration, not a point → use 'for'. Correct: 'She has been working on this project FOR three years.' TRAP: 'since' and 'for' are both time prepositions and often confused. SSC tests this distinction repeatedly.

questions.stem: The news that (A) / the prime minister had resigned (B) / have shocked everyone in the country (C). / No error (D).
questions.explanation: C is correct. Error in Part C: 'have shocked' should be 'has shocked'. RULE: The subject of this sentence is 'The news' (singular/uncountable noun — treated as singular in grammar). The clause 'that the prime minister had resigned' is a NOUN CLAUSE modifying 'news', not the subject. The verb must agree with 'news' (singular) → 'has shocked'. Correct: '...has shocked everyone.' TRAP: Students jump from 'resigned' to 'have' thinking the subject is 'prime minister', but by that point we are already back to the main clause where subject = 'The news'.

questions.stem: He is too weak (A) / to not lift (B) / even a light bag (C). / No error (D).
questions.explanation: B is correct. Error in Part B: 'to not lift' should be 'to lift'. RULE: 'Too + adjective + to + infinitive' already carries a NEGATIVE meaning ('too weak to lift' = so weak that he CANNOT lift). Adding 'not' creates an ungrammatical double negative: 'too weak to NOT lift' would paradoxically mean he is NOT able to NOT lift (i.e., he CAN lift). Correct: 'He is too weak TO LIFT even a light bag.' TRAP: Students hear the negative meaning and insert 'not', not realising 'too...to' is inherently negative.

questions.stem: Either the principal (A) / or the teachers (B) / is responsible for this decision (C). / No error (D).
questions.explanation: C is correct. Error in Part C: 'is responsible' should be 'are responsible'. RULE: With 'Either...or' / 'Neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject NEAREST to it (proximity rule). Here, the nearest subject = 'the teachers' (plural) → verb must be plural = 'are responsible'. Correct: 'Either the principal or the teachers ARE responsible...' Contrast: 'Either the teachers or the principal IS responsible' (nearest = 'the principal' = singular → 'is'). TRAP: Students see 'either...or' and assume singular subject → wrong.

questions.stem: Hardly had she arrived (A) / at the station (B) / than the train left (C). / No error (D).
questions.explanation: C is correct. Error in Part C: 'than' should be 'when'. RULE: 'Hardly/Scarcely...WHEN' and 'Barely...WHEN' — these negative adverbs require 'when' to introduce the following clause, NOT 'than'. 'No sooner...THAN' is the only pair that uses 'than'. Confusing the pairs is the classic SSC trap. Correct: 'Hardly had she arrived at the station WHEN the train left.' Note also: 'Hardly had she arrived' = correct inversion after 'hardly' at the start of a sentence. TRAP: 'No sooner + than' and 'Hardly + when' are swapped by students under exam pressure.

questions.stem: The accused denied (A) / that he had stole (B) / the money from the safe (C). / No error (D).
questions.explanation: B is correct. Error in Part B: 'stole' should be 'stolen'. RULE: 'Had + PAST PARTICIPLE' forms the past perfect tense. The past participle of 'steal' is 'STOLEN' (steal → stole → stolen). 'stole' is the simple past, not the past participle. Correct: '...that he had STOLEN the money...' Common irregular verbs SSC tests: steal-stole-stolen; break-broke-broken; freeze-froze-frozen; speak-spoke-spoken; wake-woke-woken. TRAP: Students confuse simple past (stole) with past participle (stolen); they are different forms for irregular verbs.

questions.stem: Being a rainy day, (A) / the manager decided (B) / to cancel the outdoor meeting (C). / No error (D).
questions.explanation: A is correct. Error in Part A: 'Being a rainy day' is a DANGLING MODIFIER. RULE: A participial phrase at the beginning of a sentence must logically refer to the subject of the main clause. The main clause subject = 'the manager'. So 'Being a rainy day' implies the MANAGER is a rainy day — which is absurd. Correct forms: 'It being a rainy day, the manager...' OR 'Since it was a rainy day, the manager...' Dangling modifiers are a recurrent high-difficulty error type in SSC CGL Tier 2 spotting errors. TRAP: The rest of the sentence sounds logical; the error is structural (modifier-subject mismatch), not lexical.

questions.stem: He is one of those officers (A) / who always gives priority (B) / to the welfare of his subordinates (C). / No error (D).
questions.explanation: B is correct. Error in Part B: 'gives' should be 'give'. RULE: In 'one of those + plural noun + who', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to the PLURAL noun ('officers'), not to 'one'. Therefore the verb after 'who' must be PLURAL: 'who always GIVE priority'. Compare: 'He is THE ONE officer who always GIVES priority' (here 'one officer' is singular → 'gives'). The phrase 'one of those X who' = 'who' → X (plural) → plural verb. TRAP: Students focus on 'He is one' (singular) and use 'gives' without realising 'who' modifies 'those officers' (plural).

questions.stem: The committee has been deliberating (A) / the matter since yesterday (B) / and have not yet reached a decision (C). / No error (D).
questions.explanation: C is correct. Error in Part C: 'have not yet reached' should be 'has not yet reached'. RULE: Within a SINGLE sentence, the same collective noun subject must keep the same number agreement throughout. Part A uses 'The committee HAS been deliberating' (treating committee as singular) → Part C must also use 'HAS not yet reached' to remain consistent. Switching from 'has' (Part A) to 'have' (Part C) is an internal inconsistency. Correct: '...and HAS not yet reached a decision.' TRAP: The long intervening phrase causes students to forget the original verb number used in Part A. Consistency within a sentence is a crucial Tier 2 rule.
